findings.title: Second `downsize` definition overrides the 4-arg version
findings.body: Ruby has no overloading. The new `self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` replaces the earlier `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})`. Existing callers that pass width and height separately now bind `max_height` to `opts`. That makes `opts` an Integer, so `opts[:allow_animation]` and `opts[:force_aspect_ratio]` misbehave, and the dimensions string is built from only the width. The earlier definition is dead code.

findings.title: Downsize loop ignores failure and can mis-handle animated GIFs
findings.body: The result of `OptimizedImage.downsize` is never checked. If convert fails, the loop retries the same failing command five times. The call also passes `tempfile.path` as both source and destination. For animated GIFs, gifsicle with `--resize-fit "80%"` is not a valid percentage argument. The `from =~ /\.GIF$/i` check depends on the tempfile path having an extension, which tempfiles may lack. After the loop the file may still exceed the limit and the code does not report that.

findings.title: Hardcoded 10MB limits replace the configurable size settings
findings.body: The download cap and the client-side checks in `utilities.js` are now fixed at 10MB. They no longer follow `max_image_size_kb` or `max_attachment_size_kb`. Attachment size limits are no longer enforced on the client, and the error message shows 10MB even when the site setting is lower. If the server limit is raised above 10MB, the client still blocks those uploads.

findings.title: Client-side validation no longer respects site settings
findings.body: `maxSizeKB` is hardcoded to 10MB for all types. Non-image attachments are no longer checked against `max_attachment_size_kb`. The server may then reject them after the upload has already been sent.
